entries.claim: The 1900 Galveston hurricane was the deadliest natural disaster in the history of the United States.
entries.quote: became the deadliest natural disaster in the history of the United States

entries.claim: The 1900 Galveston hurricane left between 6,000 and 12,000 fatalities.
entries.quote: left between 6,000 and 12,000 fatalities

entries.claim: The death toll most cited in official reports for the 1900 Galveston hurricane is 8,000.
entries.quote: the number most cited in official reports is 8,000

entries.claim: On September 1, 1900, Father Reese Gangoite, the director of the Belen College Observatory in Havana, noted that the storm was in its formative stages.
entries.quote: Father Reese Gangoite, the director of the Belen College Observatory in Havana, Cuba, noted that the storm was in its formative stages

entries.claim: Gangoite concluded from a persistent lunar halo, a deep red sky, and northward-moving cirrus clouds that the storm had intensified and was heading toward the coast of Texas.
entries.quote: This indicated to him that the tropical storm had intensified and that the prevailing winds were moving the system towards the coast of Texas

entries.claim: The United States Weather Bureau disagreed with Gangoite's forecast, expecting the system to recurve and make landfall in Florida before impacting the East Coast.
entries.quote: disagreed with this forecast, as they expected the system to recurve and make landfall in Florida

entries.claim: Weather Bureau director Willis Luther Moore implemented a policy to block telegraph reports from Cuban meteorologists at the Colegio de Belén in Havana due to tensions after the Spanish–American War.
entries.quote: a policy to block telegraph reports from Cuban meteorologists at the meteorological observatory of the Colegio de Belén in Havana

entries.claim: Willis Moore changed Weather Bureau protocol to force local offices to seek authorization from the central office before issuing storm warnings.
entries.quote: force local Weather Bureau offices to seek authorization from the central office before issuing storm warnings

entries.claim: On September 4, 1900, the Weather Bureau's Galveston office began receiving warnings from the central office in Washington, D.C. that a tropical disturbance had moved northward over Cuba.
entries.quote: began receiving warnings from the central office in Washington, D.C. that a tropical disturbance had moved northward over Cuba

entries.claim: The Weather Bureau discouraged the use of terms such as "hurricane" or "tornado" to avoid panicking residents in the path of a storm.
entries.quote: they discouraged the use of terms such as "hurricane" or "tornado" to avoid panicking residents in the path of any storm event

entries.claim: On September 5, 1900, the Weather Bureau's central office issued a storm warning in Florida from Cedar Key to Miami.
entries.quote: the central office of the Weather Bureau issued a storm warning in Florida from Cedar Key to Miami on September 5

entries.claim: By September 6, 1900, a hurricane warning was in effect along the coast from Cedar Key to Savannah, Georgia.
entries.quote: a hurricane warning was in effect along the coast from Cedar Key to Savannah, Georgia

entries.claim: Cuban forecasters adamantly disagreed with the Weather Bureau, saying the hurricane would continue west.
entries.quote: Cuban forecasters adamantly disagreed with the Weather Bureau, saying the hurricane would continue west

entries.claim: One Cuban forecaster predicted the hurricane would continue into central Texas near San Antonio.
entries.quote: One Cuban forecaster predicted the hurricane would continue into central Texas near San Antonio

entries.claim: On September 7, 1900, the Weather Bureau realized the storm was continuing west-northwest across the Gulf of Mexico rather than turning northward as it had predicted.
entries.quote: the Weather Bureau realized that the storm was continuing west-northwest across the Gulf of Mexico

entries.claim: Weather Bureau director Willis Luther Moore insisted that the cyclone was not of hurricane intensity.
entries.quote: Weather Bureau director Willis Luther Moore insisted that the cyclone was not of hurricane intensity

entries.claim: Isaac Cline, director of the Weather Bureau's Galveston office, wrote an 1891 article in the Galveston Daily News stating it would be impossible for a hurricane of significant strength to strike Galveston Island.
entries.quote: wrote an 1891 article in the Galveston Daily News stating it would be impossible for a hurricane of significant strength to strike Galveston Island

entries.claim: Isaac Cline is credited with issuing a hurricane warning without permission from the Weather Bureau's central office.
entries.quote: Isaac Cline is credited with issuing a hurricane warning without permission from the Bureau's central office

entries.claim: According to author Erik Larson, no other survivors are known to have corroborated Isaac Cline's accounts of warning residents before the storm.
entries.quote: according to Larson, no other survivors are known to have corroborated these accounts

entries.claim: The cyclone made landfall around 8:00 p.m. CST on September 8, 1900, to the south of Houston as a Category 4 hurricane.
entries.quote: made landfall around 8:00 p.m CST on September 8

entries.claim: On September 7, 1900, the storm reached its peak intensity with estimated sustained wind speeds of 145 mph (235 km/h).
entries.quote: On September 7, the system reached its peak intensity with estimated sustained wind speeds of 145 mph (235 km/h)

entries.claim: The hurricane brought a storm surge of over 15 ft (4.6 m) that washed over the entire island.
entries.quote: a storm surge of over 15 ft (4.6 m) that washed over the entire island

entries.claim: Isaac's Storm: A Man, a Time, and the Deadliest Hurricane in History was written by Erik Larson.
entries.quote: a 2000 New York Times bestseller by Erik Larson

entries.claim: Isaac's Storm was a New York Times bestseller in 2000.
entries.quote: is a 2000 New York Times bestseller

entries.claim: The book follows the events immediately preceding, during, and after the 1900 Galveston hurricane.
entries.quote: The book follows the events immediately preceding, during, and after the 1900 Galveston hurricane.

entries.claim: The book opens with Isaac Cline on the night of September 7, 1900, the eve of the hurricane's landfall.
entries.quote: The book opens with a restless Isaac Cline on the night of September 7, 1900

entries.claim: On the eve of the storm, Isaac Cline could not shake the uneasy feeling that something was amiss, despite meteorological signs saying otherwise.
entries.quote: despite all of the meteorological signs saying otherwise, cannot shake the uneasy feeling that something is amiss

entries.claim: The book portrays the meteorologists of Cuba as very skilled in the art.
entries.quote: The meteorologists of Cuba are shown to be very skilled in the art

entries.claim: Cuba's meteorologists were completely ignored by the overconfident Weather Bureau and its meteorologists.
entries.quote: but are completely ignored by the overconfident Weather Bureau and its meteorologists

entries.claim: The 1900 hurricane passed over Cuba.
entries.quote: The hurricane passes over Cuba

entries.claim: The Cubans predicted the storm would head towards Texas.
entries.quote: the Cubans predict it to be heading towards Texas

entries.claim: The Weather Bureau believed the storm would track towards Florida.
entries.quote: The Weather Bureau, however, disagrees and believes that the storm will track towards Florida

entries.claim: The book's narrative is supported by inserted letters and telegrams surrounding the events of the storm.
entries.quote: The narrative is supported by the insertion of letters and telegrams surrounding the events of the storm

entries.claim: The 1900 Galveston hurricane killed thousands of people.
entries.quote: the storm literally uproots half the island and kills thousands

entries.claim: The storm uprooted half the island of Galveston.
entries.quote: the storm literally uproots half the island

entries.claim: From the mainland's view, Galveston went quiet, with no news or telegrams reaching anyone.
entries.quote: Galveston goes quiet with no news or telegrams reaching anyone

entries.claim: Isaac Monroe Cline was the chief meteorologist at the Galveston, Texas office of the U.S. Weather Bureau from 1889 to 1901.
entries.quote: was the chief meteorologist at the Galveston, Texas office of the U.S. Weather Bureau from 1889 to 1901

entries.claim: Cline authored an article for the Galveston Daily News in which he derided the idea of significant hurricane damage to Galveston as "a crazy idea".
entries.quote: derided the idea of significant damage to Galveston from a hurricane as "a crazy idea"

entries.claim: Cline's article played a significant role in preventing the construction of a proposed seawall.
entries.quote: This article played a significant role in preventing the construction of a proposed seawall

entries.claim: The proposed seawall followed the destruction of the competing port of Indianola in the 1886 Indianola hurricane.
entries.quote: following the destruction of a competing port, Indianola, in the 1886 Indianola hurricane

entries.claim: Cline is credited with violating Weather Bureau policy by unilaterally issuing a hurricane warning during the 1900 hurricane.
entries.quote: violating Weather Bureau policy and unilaterally issuing a hurricane warning

entries.claim: Cline's hurricane warning came too late to allow residents to evacuate the island.
entries.quote: this warning, however, came too late to allow residents to evacuate the island

entries.claim: Cline's wife, Cora, drowned during the hurricane.
entries.quote: Cline's wife, Cora, ultimately drowning

entries.claim: Nearby Houston took over Galveston's position as the prominent port in Texas.
entries.quote: nearby Houston taking over Galveston's position as the prominent port in Texas

entries.claim: The 1900 Atlantic hurricane season featured the Galveston hurricane, the deadliest natural disaster in United States history.
entries.quote: featured the Galveston hurricane, the deadliest natural disaster in the United States history

entries.claim: A total of 10 tropical cyclones formed during the 1900 Atlantic hurricane season.
entries.quote: A total of 10 tropical cyclones formed

entries.claim: A ship encountered the season's first tropical storm early on August 27, while located about 1,160 mi (1,865 km) east of the southernmost islands of Cape Verde.
entries.quote: a ship encountered the first tropical storm of the season, while located about 1,160 mi (1,865 km) east of the southernmost islands of Cape Verde

entries.claim: The storm entered the northeastern Caribbean on August 30.
entries.quote: entered the northeastern Caribbean on August 30

entries.claim: The storm made landfall in the Dominican Republic as a weak tropical storm on September 2.
entries.quote: made landfall in Dominican Republic as a weak tropical storm on September 2

entries.claim: On September 3, the cyclone struck modern-day Santiago de Cuba Province.
entries.quote: the cyclone struck modern day Santiago de Cuba Province

entries.claim: After striking Santiago de Cuba Province, the cyclone slowly drifted along the southern coast of Cuba.
entries.quote: then slowly drifted along the southern coast of Cuba

entries.claim: The storm brought heavy rainfall to Cuba, with up to 12.58 in (320 mm) in Santiago de Cuba.
entries.quote: The storm brought heavy rainfall to Cuba, with up to 12.58 in (320 mm)

entries.claim: Upon reaching the Gulf of Mexico on September 6, the storm strengthened into a hurricane near Dry Tortugas.
entries.quote: Upon reaching the Gulf of Mexico on September 6, the storm strengthened into a hurricane, while situated near Dry Tortugas.

entries.claim: The cyclone peaked as a Category 4 hurricane with winds of 145 mph (230 km/h) on September 8.
entries.quote: peaked as a Category 4 hurricane with winds of 145 mph (230 km/h) on September 8

entries.claim: Around the time of landfall, the hurricane's minimum barometric pressure of 936 mbar (27.6 inHg) was observed.
entries.quote: its minimum barometric pressure of 936 mbar (27.6 inHg) was observed

entries.claim: Early on September 9, the hurricane made landfall near modern-day Jamaica Beach, Texas, with winds of 140 mph (225 km/h).
entries.quote: it made landfall near modern-day Jamaica Beach, Texas, with winds of 140 mph (225 km/h)

entries.claim: In Texas, strong winds were reported in the Galveston area, reaching 120 mph (195 km/h).
entries.quote: strong winds were reported in the Galveston area, reaching 120 mph (195 km/h)

entries.claim: Storm surge cresting between 8 and 15 ft (2.4 and 4.6 m) inundated the entirety of Galveston Island.
entries.quote: Storm surge cresting between 8 and 15 ft (2.4 and 4.6 m) inundated the entirety of Galveston Island.

entries.claim: The Galveston hurricane killed between 6,000 and 12,000 people.
entries.quote: killing between 6,000 and 12,000 people

entries.claim: Official estimates put the Galveston hurricane's death toll at approximately 8,000.
entries.quote: Official estimates put the death toll at approximately 8,000.

entries.claim: Every house on Galveston Island sustained damage, with at least 3,636 houses destroyed.
entries.quote: Every house sustained damage, with at least 3,636 destroyed

entries.claim: Approximately 10,000 people were left homeless in Galveston.
entries.quote: approximately 10,000 were left homeless

entries.claim: Galveston's total population at the time was 37,000.
entries.quote: out of a total population of 37,000

entries.claim: Property damage from the storm in Galveston alone was estimated at $30 million.
entries.quote: Property damage from the storm in Galveston alone was estimated at $30 million.

entries.claim: The Galveston hurricane caused about $35.5 million (1.9 billion USD) in damage overall.
entries.quote: The hurricane overall caused about $35.5 million (1.9 billion USD) in damage.

entries.claim: During Tropical Storm Four, a telegraph from the Weather Bureau headquarters in Washington, D.C. warned vessels to remain in port for portions of the Gulf Coast of the United States.
entries.quote: warned vessels to remain in port for portions of the Gulf Coast of the United States

entries.claim: The Galveston Seawall is a seawall located in Galveston, Texas.
entries.quote: The Galveston Seawall is a seawall in Galveston, Texas

entries.claim: The Galveston Seawall was built after the 1900 Galveston hurricane for protection from future hurricanes.
entries.quote: built after the 1900 Galveston hurricane for protection from future hurricanes

entries.claim: Construction of the Galveston Seawall began in September 1902.
entries.quote: Construction began in September 1902

entries.claim: The initial segment of the Galveston Seawall was completed on July 29, 1904.
entries.quote: the initial segment was completed on July 29, 1904

entries.claim: The Galveston Seawall was extended between 1904 and 1963.
entries.quote: From 1904 to 1963, the seawall was extended

entries.claim: The Galveston Seawall was extended from 3.3 miles (5.3 km) to over 10 miles (16 km).
entries.quote: extended from 3.3 miles (5.3 km) to over 10 miles (16 km)

entries.claim: Although the seawall performed as intended, it caused passive erosion resulting in the gradual disappearance of the once-wide beach and the resort business.
entries.quote: passive erosion resulting in the gradual disappearance of the once-wide beach and the resort business

entries.claim: Within twenty years of the seawall's construction, the city of Galveston had lost one hundred yards of sand.
entries.quote: Within twenty years, the city had lost one hundred yards of sand.

entries.claim: Houston soon overtook Galveston as the major city in the region.
entries.quote: Houston soon overtook Galveston as the major city in the region.

entries.claim: Hurricane Alicia occurred in 1983.
entries.quote: the 1983 Hurricane Alicia

entries.claim: Reporting in the aftermath of Hurricane Alicia, the Corps of Engineers estimated that $100 million in damage was avoided because of the seawall.
entries.quote: estimated that $100 million in damage was avoided because of the seawall

entries.claim: On September 13, 2008, large waves from Hurricane Ike over-topped the Galveston Seawall.
entries.quote: On September 13, 2008, Hurricane Ike's large waves over-topped the seawall

entries.claim: As a result of Hurricane Ike over-topping the seawall, a commission was established by the Texas governor to investigate preparing for and mitigating future disasters.
entries.quote: a commission was established by the Texas governor to investigate preparing for and mitigating future disasters

entries.claim: A proposal has been put forth to build an "Ike Dike", a massive levee system that would protect Galveston Bay and industrial facilities along the coast and the Houston Ship Channel from a future, potentially more destructive storm.
entries.quote: a massive levee system that would protect the Galveston Bay

entries.claim: The Ike Dike proposal never passed the conceptual stage.
entries.quote: this proposal never passed the conceptual stage

entries.claim: Since 2009, proposals for a layered network of smaller, local levees and natural protections have been put forward by the SSPEED Center at Rice University and the University of Houston.
entries.quote: the SSPEED Center at Rice University and the University of Houston

entries.claim: Texas F.M. 3005 is known as Seawall Boulevard where it runs along the seawall.
entries.quote: Texas F.M. 3005 is known as Seawall Boulevard where it runs along the seawall

entries.claim: The sidewalk on top of the seawall adjacent to Seawall Boulevard is claimed to be the longest continuous sidewalk in the world, at 10.3 miles (16.6 km) long.
entries.quote: claimed to be the longest continuous sidewalk in the world at 10.3 miles (16.6 km) long

entries.claim: The Galveston Seawall is approximately 17 feet (5.2 m) high.
entries.quote: approximately 17 feet (5.2 m) high

entries.claim: The Galveston Seawall is approximately 16 feet (4.9 m) thick at its base.
entries.quote: 16 feet (4.9 m) thick at its base

entries.claim: The Galveston Seawall was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1977.
entries.quote: listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1977

entries.claim: The Galveston Seawall was designated a National Historic Civil Engineering Landmark by the American Society of Civil Engineers in 2001.
entries.quote: designated a National Historic Civil Engineering Landmark by the American Society of Civil Engineers in 2001
